item.title: Daimonzaka: The Moss-Covered Pilgrim Stairway to Nachi — Guide
item.description: Daimonzaka is the single most beautiful short section of the entire Kumano Kodo: a 600-metre stairway of moss-covered stone steps climbing through a corridor of towering cedars, some of them 800 years old, toward Kumano Nachi Taisha and the falls. Two giant cedars known as the ‘husband and wife trees’ frame the entrance, and the green light filtering down through the canopy gives the climb an unmistakably sacred atmosphere. Taking only about 30 minutes, it lets any visitor walk a genuine stretch of World Heritage pilgrim path — and local shops even rent Heian-period pilgrim costumes for the walk.

item.title: Okunoin: Japan's Largest Cemetery Beneath the Cedars — Guide
item.description: Okunoin is the spiritual climax of Koyasan and the largest cemetery in Japan: a two-kilometre path winding beneath towering, centuries-old cedars past some 200,000 tombstones, memorials and mossy stupas, from feudal lords and famous samurai to company memorials and modern graves. At its far end stands the Gobyo, the mausoleum of Kobo Daishi, who is believed by the faithful not to have died but to rest in eternal meditation, awaiting the future Buddha — monks still carry him meals twice daily.

item.title: Okuno-in Cedar Forest Walk: A Quiet Sacred Grove — Guide
item.description: The Okuno-in cedar forest walk is a peaceful trail through a grove of towering old cedar trees leading to a secluded okuno-in, the ‘inner sanctuary’ traditionally set deep behind a temple’s main halls, where the atmosphere of filtered light, moss and massive trunks makes the walk itself the point. Well off Shizuoka’s main tourist routes, it offers a quiet forest-bathing escape, the kind of unhurried, contemplative woodland stroll that rewards travellers looking beyond the famous sights.

item.title: Kashima Jingu: Complete Guide to Ibaraki's Ancient Shrine
item.description: In a prefecture better known abroad for blue nemophila fields and a giant Buddha, Kashima Jingu stands apart as one of Japan’s most historically charged sacred sites. Buried deep in a forest of ancient Japanese cedar on the Pacific coast of eastern Ibaraki, the shrine predates written Japanese history. It was founded, according to tradition, in the reign of the legendary Emperor Jimmu, making it roughly contemporary with the origin myths of the Japanese state itself.
